chapter.name: Surface Areas and Volumes
chapter.blurb: A truck's oil tank, a test tube, a birthday top and Mayank's garden bird-bath share one feature: none of them is a single cuboid, cone, cylinder or sphere, but each is built by combining two or more of these. This chapter develops the bookkeeping needed for such composite solids -- for total surface area, working out exactly which flat circular faces vanish at a join, survive untouched, or are only partly covered (leaving an exposed ring when the two radii differ), so that curved surfaces are added but no vanished face is double-counted; and for volume, where this bookkeeping problem never arises and the parts' volumes simply add. It then applies this to practical questions -- a glass's true capacity once a raised base is allowed for, the wood left after drilling pen-holder depressions, the number of lead shots a vessel's water can absorb, and a solid's mass from its density. This rationalized edition restricts itself to the five basic solids named in its own opening section (cuboid, cone, cylinder, sphere, hemisphere) and to combinations of exactly two at a time; it closes with a two-point Summary and does not go on to the frustum of a cone or to converting one solid into another of equal volume, both part of the pre-2023 edition's longer version of this chapter.

Find the volume of a solid formed by combining two or more basic solids by adding the volumes of the individual parts

Use the volume of a combination solid to find a practical derived quantity: actual capacity after removing a hollow part, quantity of material used or remaining, volume of a liquid displaced or left over, mass from density, or checking whether a stated capacity is correct

concepts.name: Surface area of solids joined by matching curved surfaces (CSA addition)
concepts.description: Finding the total surface area (TSA) of a solid formed by joining two or more basic solids (cone, cylinder, sphere, hemisphere) at matching circular faces of the SAME radius, so that neither joining face stays exposed and only curved surfaces remain visible.
concepts.idea: When two curved solids of the same radius are joined so that neither flat circular face is left exposed in the final shape, that flat area is not part of the outer surface at all -- the total surface area is just the sum of the curved surface areas of the visible parts.
concepts.rule: TSA(combination) = sum of the CSAs of the curved parts only, when every flat circular face involved is at a join (and vanishes) or is otherwise not exposed. CSA(hemisphere) = 2 pi r^2, CSA(cone) = pi r l where l = sqrt(r^2 + h^2), CSA(cylinder) = 2 pi r h. Never add either joining face's own flat circular area. This applies whether the curved piece is stuck ON (a bump) or scooped OUT (a depression), since either way the same flat area vanishes and the same curved area appears.
concepts.example: Rasheed's playing top (Example 1) is a cone (radius 1.75 cm) mounted on a hemisphere of the same radius: TSA = CSA(cone) + CSA(hemisphere) = pi r l + 2 pi r^2, about 39.6 cm^2 (using pi = 22/7).

Verifies: curved surface area of cone = 11 x 7.4 = 81.4 cm^2, curved surface area of hemisphere = 11 x 7 = 77 cm^2, total = 158.4 cm^2, matching the target

concepts.name: Surface area with a flat face added or removed at the join
concepts.description: Finding the total surface area of a solid formed by attaching a curved piece (a hemisphere or a cone) to, or removing one from, a solid that has genuine flat faces of its own (a cube, a cuboid, or a cylinder's flat end), where exactly one circular patch of that flat face is replaced by the curved piece's own curved surface.
concepts.idea: A flat-faced solid keeps all its OTHER faces when a curved piece is attached to or scooped from just one face -- only that one face loses a circular patch, which is replaced by the curved surface of the attached or removed piece.
concepts.rule: TSA(combination) = TSA(original flat-faced solid) - (circular patch removed, pi r^2) + (curved surface area of the attached/removed piece, e.g. 2 pi r^2 for a hemisphere or pi r l for a cone). Every other face of the original solid is unaffected and still counts in full. This is the same whether the curved piece sticks out or is scooped in.
concepts.example: The decorative block (Example 2) is a cube of edge 5 cm with a hemisphere of radius 2.1 cm fixed on top: TSA = 6(5)^2 - pi(2.1)^2 + 2 pi(2.1)^2 = 163.86 cm^2 (using pi = 22/7).

concepts.name: Surface area when joined radii differ: the exposed ring correction
concepts.description: Finding the total surface area of a solid formed by joining two curved solids of DIFFERENT radii (such as a cone and a cylinder), where the wider solid's flat face is only partly covered by the narrower one, leaving a flat ring (annulus) exposed that must be added to both curved surfaces.
concepts.idea: When the two joined solids do not share the same radius, their join can no longer hide both flat faces completely -- part of the wider face stays exposed as a ring, and this ring's area is real, visible area that has to be counted alongside both curved surfaces.
concepts.rule: If the two radii are R (wider) and r (narrower), the exposed ring has area pi(R^2 - r^2) = pi(R - r)(R + r). The total surface area adds this ring to both curved surfaces (and to any other genuinely exposed flat face, such as an open end). If R = r, the ring vanishes and this reduces to the same-radius case.
concepts.example: Rasheed's rocket (Example 3) is a cone of radius 2.5 cm on a cylinder of radius 1.5 cm: the area to be painted orange is the cone's curved surface plus the exposed ring on the cone's own base, pi(2.5^2 - 1.5^2), giving about 63.585 cm^2 (using pi = 3.14).

concepts.name: Volume of a combination of solids: adding the parts' volumes
concepts.description: Finding the volume of a solid made by joining two or more basic solids (cuboid, cone, cylinder, sphere, hemisphere) by adding the volumes of the individual parts; unlike surface area, no part of the volume is ever subtracted merely because the solids are joined.
concepts.idea: Volume measures the space a solid encloses, not its outer skin, so joining two solids together never makes any of that enclosed space disappear -- the combination's volume is simply the sum of the parts' volumes.
concepts.rule: Volume(combination) = Volume(part 1) + Volume(part 2) + ..., using Volume(cuboid) = lbh, Volume(cylinder) = pi r^2 h, Volume(cone) = (1/3) pi r^2 h, Volume(sphere) = (4/3) pi r^3, Volume(hemisphere) = (2/3) pi r^3. This holds whatever the radii of the parts are, and never needs a subtraction for the join itself, since a flat face has no volume.
concepts.example: A solid toy is a cone (height 2 cm, radius 2 cm) mounted on a hemisphere of the same radius (Example 7): volume = (1/3) pi (2)^2(2) + (2/3) pi (2)^3 = 25.12 cm^3 (using pi = 3.14).

concepts.name: Volume in practice: capacity, material used, displacement and mass
concepts.description: Using the volume of a combination solid to answer a practical question: the actual capacity of a container once a hollow or raised part is allowed for, the quantity of material used or left after removing a part, the volume of liquid displaced or remaining, the mass of a solid via its density, or checking whether a stated capacity is correct.
concepts.idea: Once you can find a combination solid's volume, many real questions ask you to go one step further: subtract a hollowed-out or occupied part to get the volume that is actually usable, or convert that volume into a different practical quantity such as mass or a count of identical pieces.
concepts.rule: Actual/usable volume = (bulk or apparent volume) - (volume of any hollow, raised or occupied part). Mass = density x volume. Number of identical pieces from a displaced volume = (displaced volume) / (volume of one piece). To check a stated capacity, independently compute the geometric volume from the given dimensions and compare it with the claim.
concepts.example: A glass is a cylinder (radius 2.5 cm, height 10 cm) with a hemispherical bump of the same radius raised at its base (Example 6): actual capacity = pi r^2 h - (2/3) pi r^3 = 196.25 - 32.71 = 163.54 cm^3 (approx, using pi = 3.14).

questions.q: A cylindrical glass of radius 2 cm and height 9 cm has a hemispherical bump of the same radius raised at its base. A shopkeeper claims the glass holds 100 cm^3 of liquid. Using pi = 22/7, evaluate whether this claim is accurate.
questions.a: The claim is not accurate. The actual capacity works out to about 96.38 cm^3 (apparent capacity about 113.14 cm^3 minus the hemisphere's volume about 16.76 cm^3), so the shopkeeper has overstated the capacity by about 3.6 cm^3.
s: Computes apparent capacity = pi r^2 h = (22/7)(4)(9) = about 113.14 cm^3, and hemisphere volume = (2/3) pi r^3 = about 16.76 cm^3
Finds actual capacity = about 96.38 cm^3 and concludes the shopkeeper's claim of 100 cm^3 overstates this, so the claim is not accurate

questions.q: Design a glass in the shape of a cylinder of radius 3 cm with a hemispherical bump of the same radius raised at its base, so that its actual capacity is exactly 36 pi cm^3. Find a suitable height for the cylinder, and verify your answer.
questions.a: Height = 6 cm. Apparent capacity = 54 pi cm^3, hemisphere volume = 18 pi cm^3, actual capacity = 36 pi cm^3.
s: Sets up apparent capacity = pi(3)^2 h = 9 pi h, hemisphere volume = (2/3) pi (27) = 18 pi, and equates 9 pi h - 18 pi = 36 pi
Cancels pi and solves 9h - 18 = 36, giving h = 6 cm
Verifies: apparent = 9 pi(6) = 54 pi, actual = 54 pi - 18 pi = 36 pi cm^3, matching the target
